preamble: Denasalization of the glottalized alveolar nasal [nˀ] (Americanist n̓) to plain [d]. In Makah the Proto-Southern-Wakashan (PSW) nasals became voiced stops and the glottalized sonorants merged with the plain ones, lengthening the preceding vowel (Davidson 2002: 76, citing Jacobsen 1968). PSW *n̓ therefore appears as Makah d, while Nuu-chah-nulth keeps n̓: Nuu-chah-nulth čun̓a, Makah ču·da 'vulva', from Proto-Nootkan *ču(ː)n̍a in Fortescue's reconstruction as listed on Wiktionary. The same correspondence recurs in suffixes listed by Davidson. For Quileute, Wikipedia's summary of Powell (1974) gives Proto-Chimakuan *n̓ > Quileute d or ʔd (Chemakum n or ʔn), without a word example. Ditidaht has the same plain d word-initially, where its glottalized d̓ cannot occur: Proto-Wakashan *n̓ak- 'look' gives Nuu-chah-nulth n̓ač- but Ditidaht and Makah dač- (Howe & Pulleyblank 2001). After a vowel Ditidaht keeps the glottalization as d̓.

languageExamples.context: Davidson (2002: 76): the Proto-Southern-Wakashan glottalized sonorants merged with the plain sonorants in Makah, with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (citing Jacobsen 1968); Nuu-chah-nulth keeps them; the nasal also became a stop, as plain *n did. Werle (2010: 4) lists the "loss of glottalized resonants in Makah with concomitant lengthening of a preceding vowel" and describes "the change from nasals to voiced plosives in Ditidaht and Makah"

examples.note: Davidson (2002: 76), ex. (127), beside Nuu-chah-nulth čun̓a 'vulva'. The long u· before d is the compensatory lengthening. Proto-Nootkan form after Fortescue (2007), from the Wiktionary appendix of Proto-Wakashan reconstructions, which lists no descendants; it writes n̍ for n̓.
Davidson (2002: 202), ex. (300), beside Nuu-chah-nulth -n̓a·qi 'up on a height'. Proto-Nootkan form after Fortescue (2007), Wiktionary appendix.
Howe & Pulleyblank (2001), ex. (30a), p. 22 of the accepted manuscript, citing Howe (1999), beside Nuu-chah-nulth n̓ač- and Ditidaht dač-. Werle (2010: 9), ex. (23), has Makah dačʔoł 'see'.

languageExamples.context: Word-initially, where Ditidaht d̓ cannot stand: Werle (2010: 5) says glottalized b̓ d̓ must follow a vowel. Initial *n̓ gives plain d, merging with *n. Werle (2010: 4) calls it "the change from nasals to voiced plosives in Ditidaht and Makah"

examples.note: Howe & Pulleyblank (2001), ex. (30a), p. 22 of the accepted manuscript, which reconstructs Proto-Wakashan *n̓ak- 'look' (citing Howe 1999), beside Kwak'wala n̓ak-. Makah also has dač-. Plain *naq- 'drink' gives Ditidaht and Makah daq-. Werle (2010: 9), ex. (23), has Ditidaht dačooʔł, Makah dačʔoł 'see'. The Wiktionary appendix of Fortescue's (2007) reconstructions instead gives 'drink' a glottalized nasal, Proto-Wakashan *n̍a(ː)q-.
Werle (2010: 17), ex. (71), where the set illustrates vowel absence. Makah has duˑwiqs; its long uˑ reflects the lost glottalization of *w̓, not of *n̓.
